title: ABA Model Rule 1.1: Competence, with Official Comments
pub: ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct
author: American Bar Association

dom.t: Technology competence: Delegation preserves professional responsibility

st.t: AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core view that technology and cross-firm delegation remain governed by continuing competence, provider scrutiny and coordinated responsibility. It also confirms that responsibility allocations may be qualified by additional legal obligations, but it does not address the cluster’s distinction between retained responsibility and automatic disciplinary liability.
qs: ### Maintaining Competence  [8] To maintain the requisite knowledge and skill, a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology, engage in continuing study and education and comply with all continuing legal education requirements to which the lawyer is subject.

[7] When lawyers from more than one law firm are providing legal services to the client on a particular matter, the lawyers ordinarily should consult with each other and the client about the scope of their respective representations and the allocation of responsibility among them.

st.t: Technology competence: Delegation preserves professional responsibility
st.an: Model Rule 1.1 directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that technology and delegation operate within continuing duties of competent, ethical representation. It requires awareness of relevant technology’s benefits and risks and conditions use of outside lawyers on informed client consent and a reasonable competence-and-ethics assessment, though it does not supply AI-specific procedures or the cluster’s broader nonlawyer safeguards.
qs: ### Maintaining Competence  [8] To maintain the requisite knowledge and skill, a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology, engage in continuing study and education and comply with all continuing legal education requirements to which the lawyer is subject.

### Retaining or Contracting With Other Lawyers  [6] Before a lawyer retains or contracts with other lawyers outside the lawyer’s own firm to provide or assist in the provision of legal services to a client, the lawyer should ordinarily obtain informed consent from the client and must reasonably believe that the other lawyers’ services will contribute to the competent and ethical representation of the client.

kp.k: Competence requires knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation
kp.d: Rule 1.1 imposes a general professional duty to provide competent representation. The required standard comprises legal knowledge and skill as well as the thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the particular representation.
qs: A lawyer shall provide competent representation to a client.
Competent representation requires the legal knowledge, skill, thoroughness and preparation reasonably necessary for the representation.

kp.d: Whether a lawyer possesses sufficient knowledge and skill depends on factors including the matter’s complexity and specialization, the lawyer’s experience and training, available preparation and study, and the feasibility of consulting or associating with competent counsel. Specialized expertise is required only in some circumstances.
qs: In determining whether a lawyer employs the requisite knowledge and skill in a particular matter, relevant factors include the relative complexity and specialized nature of the matter, the lawyer's general experience, the lawyer's training and experience in the field in question, the preparation and study the lawyer is able to give the matter and whether it is feasible to refer the matter to, or associate or consult with, a lawyer of established competence in the field in question.
In many instances, the required proficiency is that of a general practitioner.
Expertise in a particular field of law may be required in some circumstances.

kp.k: Lawyers may gain competence through study or collaboration
kp.d: Prior experience or specialist training is not invariably necessary. A lawyer may become competent in an unfamiliar or novel field through necessary study, reasonable preparation, or association with a lawyer already competent in that field; newly admitted lawyers can therefore be as competent as experienced practitioners.
qs: A lawyer need not necessarily have special training or prior experience to handle legal problems of a type with which the lawyer is unfamiliar.
A newly admitted lawyer can be as competent as a practitioner with long experience.
A lawyer can provide adequate representation in a wholly novel field through necessary study.
Competent representation can also be provided through the association of a lawyer of established competence in the field in question.
A lawyer may accept representation where the requisite level of competence can be achieved by reasonable preparation.

kp.k: Core legal skills transcend specialized subject knowledge
kp.d: The comments identify precedent analysis, evidence evaluation and legal drafting as skills common to all legal problems. They characterize recognizing what kinds of legal problems a situation may involve as perhaps the most fundamental and broadly transferable legal skill.
qs: Some important legal skills, such as the analysis of precedent, the evaluation of evidence and legal drafting, are required in all legal problems.
Perhaps the most fundamental legal skill consists of determining what kind of legal problems a situation may involve, a skill that necessarily transcends any particular specialized knowledge.

kp.k: Competent work requires factual and legal inquiry
kp.d: Competence includes inquiry into and analysis of a matter’s factual and legal elements, use of methods and procedures meeting competent-practitioner standards, and adequate preparation. The degree of attention required varies with complexity, consequences and what is at stake, while an agreed limitation on representation may narrow the lawyer’s responsibilities.
qs: Competent handling of a particular matter includes inquiry into and analysis of the factual and legal elements of the problem, and use of methods and procedures meeting the standards of competent practitioners.
It also includes adequate preparation.

The required attention and preparation are determined in part by what is at stake; major litigation and complex transactions ordinarily require more extensive treatment than matters of lesser complexity and consequence.
An agreement between the lawyer and the client regarding the scope of the representation may limit the matters for which the lawyer is responsible.

kp.k: External lawyers require consent and competence assessment
kp.d: Before retaining lawyers outside the firm, a lawyer should ordinarily obtain the client’s informed consent and must reasonably believe the external lawyers will support competent and ethical representation. Relevant considerations include their education, experience and reputation, the assigned work, and jurisdictional protections and ethical environments, especially concerning confidential information.
qs: Before a lawyer retains or contracts with other lawyers outside the lawyer’s own firm to provide or assist in the provision of legal services to a client, the lawyer should ordinarily obtain informed consent from the client and must reasonably believe that the other lawyers’ services will contribute to the competent and ethical representation of the client.

The reasonableness of the decision to retain or contract with other lawyers outside the lawyer’s own firm will depend upon the circumstances, including the education, experience and reputation of the nonfirm lawyers; the nature of the services assigned to the nonfirm lawyers; and the legal protections, professional conduct rules, and ethical environments of the jurisdictions in which the services will be performed, particularly relating to confidential information.

kp.d: When multiple firms serve the same client on a matter, the lawyers ordinarily should consult with one another and the client regarding each firm’s scope and the allocation of responsibility. Tribunal matters may create additional legal obligations beyond the professional-conduct rules.
qs: When lawyers from more than one law firm are providing legal services to the client on a particular matter, the lawyers ordinarily should consult with each other and the client about the scope of their respective representations and the allocation of responsibility among them.
When making allocations of responsibility in a matter pending before a tribunal, lawyers and parties may have additional obligations that are a matter of law beyond the scope of these Rules.

kp.k: Technology benefits and risks form continuing competence
kp.d: The maintaining-competence comment expressly includes keeping abreast of the benefits and risks of relevant technology, alongside changes in law and practice, continuing study and education, and applicable continuing legal education. The document does not identify AI specifically or prescribe particular technology-verification procedures.
qs: To maintain the requisite knowledge and skill, a lawyer should keep abreast of changes in the law and its practice, including the benefits and risks associated with relevant technology, engage in continuing study and education and comply with all continuing legal education requirements to which the lawyer is subject.

pts.k: The source makes no explicit AI-specific claim or prediction. Its relevant statement is a general professional standard concerning technological competence.
pts.d: The ABA's Official Comment [8] states that maintaining competence includes keeping abreast of the benefits and risks of relevant technology. It does not name AI, predict changes to legal work or markets, or require adoption of a particular technology. Applying this statement specifically to AI would be an interpretation rather than an express claim in this document.

pts.k: The basis is professional normative authority, not empirical evidence about AI.
pts.d: The source is ABA Model Rule 1.1 and its Official Comments. The technology-related statement elaborates the general competence standard; no AI data, benchmarks, cases or adoption outcomes are offered. The document does not establish adoption or enforceability in any particular jurisdiction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Maintaining technological awareness is framed as ongoing, with no AI adoption timeline.
pts.d: Comment [8] concerns continuing maintenance of knowledge and skill and qualifies the technology reference as technology that is relevant. The general competence standard is tied to what is reasonably necessary for the representation. The supplied document's 2026 date is not a prediction horizon or a stated effective date for jurisdiction-specific obligations.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The standard addresses lawyers and the clients receiving their representation, without AI-specific market segmentation.
pts.d: Lawyers are the subjects of the competence standard and the guidance on keeping abreast of relevant technology; clients are the recipients of competent representation. The source identifies no distinct AI effects on junior lawyers, firm types, legal departments, vendors or legal-service markets.
